rv.q: When the dancers are leaping, the accordions wheezing, the lights flashing, the skirts swirling, and the vodka flowing, then Natasha, Pierre and the Great Comet of 1812 feels thrillingly unlike anything else on Broadway.
But Dave Malloy’s Natasha, Pierre & The Great Comet of 1812 feels like a party from start to end: lively, intelligent and utterly engrossing.
But this maverick show and its boundlessly inventive production are no less audacious or satisfying in their bid to rejuvenate the American musical.
It is both the most innovative and the best new musical to open on Broadway since “Hamilton,” and an inspiring sign that the commercial theater can continue to make room for the new.
No matter where you’re seated, you’re never far from the action because the action is all over the theater.
The show's eagerness to delight every last audience member is impossible to resist.
Dave Malloy's musical adaptation of a section of Tolstoy's War and Peace is a thrilling theatrical experience that makes ingenious use of its immersive staging at the Imperial Theatre.
Once again we find ourselves transported into a self-contained world where ardent Russian aristocrats and head-over-heels passion still thrive.
Especially when combined with Malloy's quirky, unconventional and thoroughly beguiling suite of songs.
Rather, Groban proves to be a thoroughly winning team player in an offbeat pop opera that is ultimately more memorable for technical dexterity than emotional texture.

It’s pure showmanship with none of the emotional payoff.
I freely acknowledge the extreme cleverness and originality of 'The Great Comet.' I just wish it didn't seem at least 45 minutes longer than it really is.
One of the most thrilling Broadway musicals this decade, The Great Comet is intimate yet epic, ironic yet deeply felt, cosmic yet down to earth.
If you like the idea of a big, bawdy, lively musical that leaves you haunted by the philosophical dilemma of its characters' place in the universe, Great Comet is your kind of show.

"A musical unlike anything else on Broadway...As incredible as the set is, though, it's not the star. That billing belongs, not to the velvet-voiced pop star Josh Groban who plays Pierre, but to Broadway newcomer Denée Benton. Benton sparkles as Natasha...Whimsy and wit permeates 'The Great Comet.' It's a dazzling production.
Groban is defintely a great addition to the Broadway theater.
The performers, including the band, make the show both serious and fun.
Great, extravagantly entertaining fun, with a soaring score that runs the musical gamut from raucous rock to classical.
Still, the show is bold and affecting and a welcome addition to the Great White Way.
Inextricable from the music and story are the overwhelming sets and costumes — sensory overload with little on its mind except offbeat entertainment.
But one senses even Tolstoy himself might have had a good chuckle over this irreverent take on a small slice of his epic novel.
The end result feels a little too much like zero-calorie entertainment: brisk and sexy and emotionally weightless.
“The Great Comet” team has managed something unusual for Broadway, an intimate and affecting musical that can’t really be said to have populist appeal.
Since it premiered, I have always found the show to be extremely uneven, with a stop-and-start momentum that alternates between all-out liveliness and long episodes of slow tedium.

As well as being a visually and kinetically riotous lark, it wants to be something deeper—as it well might, being derived from War and Peace—and that is both its charm and, amid all the jostling colors and volume, its problem.
Chavkin never stops spoofing his material, which is the major saving grace of this 'Comet.'
It's excellent at what it does, but, for all the splash, it's not clear that what it does ultimately matters all that much.
All this action — abetted by Bradley King’s spectacular lighting design, with more exquisite variations than a Disney animated film — delivers pleasure for the eye and, intermittently, the ear.
Don your finest fur and head to the theater for one of the finest productions of the year.

Natasha, Pierre & The Great Comet of 1812 is not to be missed, and with the arrival of other sung-through shows such as Murder Ballad and Here Lies Love which also take place in environments built specifically for their material, we may be at the dawning of a new kind of musical theater.
“The Great Comet” could not be more timely and compellingly relevant.
So fill your bellies ahead of time and let this dazzling show fill your spirits all night long.
